arXiv:2605.18871v1 [cs.LG] 15 May 2026

Distributional Energy-Based Models for
Uncertainty-Aware Structured LLM Reasoning

Shireen Kudukkil Manchingal ††thanks: Corresponding author: shireen.manchingal@oxdynamics.com Affiliation: Shebin Rawther    Abhey Kalia Affiliation: Oxford Dynamics    Fernanda Gonçalves Affiliation: Harwell Science and Innovation Campus, United Kingdom
Abstract

When Large Language Models produce structured outputs such as travel plans, code solutions, or multi-step proofs, individual reasoning steps may appear correct while the output as a whole violates budgets, fails test cases, or contradicts earlier deductions. We propose a decomposed energy function that combines a learned quality scorer with deterministic analytical constraint penalties for verifying structured LLM outputs. The quality scorer is a heterogeneous ensemble of low-rank adapters on a single frozen encoder (3% trainable parameters); the ensemble mean ranks candidates while the standard deviation quantifies epistemic uncertainty, driving a two-pass inference loop that triggers targeted regeneration or abstention. Across five benchmarks (GSM8K, MuSR, TravelPlanner, TACO, Knights & Knaves), our 149M-parameter verifier orchestrating a pool of 7–26B open generators outperforms single-shot Qwen-72B on every benchmark, matches Claude Sonnet 4.6 on MuSR (67.7% vs. 68.0%), and reduces constraint violations by 53% relative to Opus 4.6 on TravelPlanner (oracle 0.028, random 0.231). The two routes are complementary: structural verification wins when constraints are checkable (the verifier captures signal frontier models cannot self-detect), while pretraining-scale priors win where they are not (narrative inference, code semantics). A cross-dataset confounding analysis confirms genuine quality discrimination on four reasoning tasks and identifies a model-identity shortcut on code, mitigated via last-layer retraining. Scorers trained on difficult data transfer zero-shot: a MuSR-trained scorer achieves 93.9% on GSM8K without seeing a math problem.

1 Introduction

Large Language Models have advanced rapidly, achieving strong performance across translation, summarisation, code generation, and open-ended dialogue (Brown et al., 2020; OpenAI, 2023). A central driver of this progress is reasoning: the ability to decompose a problem into intermediate steps and arrive at a justified conclusion. Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting (Wei et al., 2022; Kojima et al., 2022) unlocked this capability by eliciting step-by-step reasoning traces, and subsequent work has extended it through self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023), least-to-most decomposition (Zhou et al., 2023), and tree-structured search (Yao et al., 2023).

Yet reasoning in current models remains fundamentally limited by the autoregressive generation mechanism: each token is committed in sequence, with no global scoring function to evaluate whether the output as a whole is consistent. Local correctness at each step does not compose into global correctness for structured outputs: cross-step violations are aggregation errors that exist only at the whole-output level (a budget exceeded only when all days are summed, a return-type mismatch propagating between functions, a single arithmetic error invalidating the rest of a derivation), and per-step scoring cannot detect them by construction, no matter how accurate. Each step receives a local correctness signal yet cross-step violations remain invisible (Fig. 1, left), so the wrong plan is delivered with no warning. GPT-4-Turbo satisfies all constraints on TravelPlanner only 4.4% of the time (Xie et al., 2024b), and even frontier models frequently produce code that fails on edge cases in competitive programming benchmarks (Chen et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023).

The bottleneck, however, is not generation but selection: pass@NN substantially exceeds pass@1, the correct candidate is usually somewhere in the pool of NN samples from the same LLM, yet existing scorers cannot reliably identify it (Brown et al., 2024; Stiennon et al., 2020). Process reward models (Lightman et al., 2023; Khalifa and others, 2025) score individual reasoning steps rather than complete outputs. Energy-based models (EBMs) offer a more natural framework for whole-output scoring, assigning low energy to good candidates and high energy to bad ones (LeCun et al., 2006), and recent work applies this principle to rerank reasoning traces (Jiang and others, 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Tan and Hong, 2025). Yet existing methods share two limitations: (i) they produce point-estimate scores with no indication of reliability (Gleave and Irving, 2022), offering no signal for when to trust, regenerate, or abstain; and (ii) they operate on flat reasoning chains with no mechanism for verifying domain-specific constraints exactly.

In this paper, we show that this selection problem can be addressed with a small specialised verifier rather than by scaling the generator. We propose a decomposed, distributional energy function E=μquality+λ⋅EconstraintE=\mu_{\text{quality}}+\lambda\cdot E_{\text{constraint}} (Fig. 1, right) combining a learned quality term μquality\mu_{\text{quality}} with deterministic analytical constraint penalties EconstraintE_{\text{constraint}}. The same compact architecture works across five fundamentally different reasoning tasks (math, narrative inference, multi-constraint planning, executable code, formal logic). The quality term μquality\mu_{\text{quality}} is realised as a heterogeneous ensemble of KK low-rank adapters (LoRA; Hu et al., 2022) on a single frozen encoder, structurally diverse so that ensemble disagreement reflects genuine epistemic uncertainty rather than superficial variation from random seeds (Fort et al., 2019; Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017; Gal and Ghahramani, 2016). The ensemble mean ranks candidates; the standard deviation σquality\sigma_{\text{quality}} drives a two-pass inference loop that triggers regeneration with structured feedback under uncertainty or constraint violations, and abstains in the extreme case. Crucially, the verifier is architecturally independent of the candidate generators, so its judgement does not collapse when the generators’ self-reported reasoning is wrong.

The following are the main contributions of this paper:

  • •

    A novel modular energy decomposition with zero-shot transfer. A transferable learned quality scorer EqualityE_{\text{quality}} and swappable deterministic penalties EconstraintE_{\text{constraint}}: EqualityE_{\text{quality}} wins beyond pretraining-scale priors, EconstraintE_{\text{constraint}} wins on checkable constraints. The scorer transfers zero-shot (MuSR-trained reaches 93.9% on GSM8K without seeing math); new tasks need only new constraint functions.

  • •

    A novel distributional energy via heterogeneous LoRA ensemble. A parameter-efficient ensemble of structurally diverse low-rank adapters produces an energy distribution rather than a point estimate, enabling confounding diagnostics and σ\sigma-gated abstention.

  • •

    Honest confounding analysis with causal verification. On 4/5 tasks the scorer learns content-based quality with no model-identity shortcut (cross-model energy spreads <0.25<0.25, picks near-uniform across generators); on TACO, a causal style-swap test exposes a formatting shortcut, fixed by last-layer retraining (Kirichenko et al., 2023) at no accuracy cost. Multi-model candidate diversity substantially improves selection.

Paper outline. Sec. 2 reviews chain-of-thought reasoning, energy-based models, reward modelling, and test-time compute. Sec. 3 presents the energy decomposition (3.1), the distributional quality scorer with formal propositions (3.2), training (3.3), analytical constraint penalties (3.4), and two-pass σ\sigma-triage (3.5). Sec. 4 reports the experimental setup (4.1) and results across all five benchmarks (4.2). Sec. 5 distils lessons learned and outlines future directions. The appendix provides proofs (§A), model and implementation details (§B, §C), dataset details and per-model candidate quality (§D, §E), and extended results: ablations (§F.1), energy diagnostics (§F.2), per-difficulty breakdowns (§F.3), selective prediction (§F.4), two-pass analysis (§F.5), per-constraint frontier comparison (§F.6), the full transfer matrix (§F.7), confounding analysis (§F.8), and broader impact (§G).

2 Related Work

Chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022; Kojima et al., 2022) elicits step-by-step reasoning; self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023), least-to-most prompting (Zhou et al., 2023), and Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al., 2023) extend it via marginalisation, decomposition, and branching search. Process reward models give finer-grained supervision: Uesato et al. (2022) and Lightman et al. (2023) show step-level outperforms outcome-level verification, and Khalifa and others (2025) train models that generate reasoning traces before scoring, with a fraction of process labels. All produce point-estimate scores on flat reasoning chains, with no mechanism for verifying that structured multi-section outputs satisfy global constraints jointly.

Energy-based models assign scalar energies to input-output pairs (LeCun et al., 2006) and have been applied to text generation (Deng et al., 2020); Blondel et al. (2025) prove autoregressive language models are themselves EBMs, and Carbone (2024) survey the broader landscape. For reasoning, Jiang and others (2025) rerank CoT on GSM8K/MATH (90.7%, 55M params); Chen et al. (2025) apply energy-based calibration to implicit CoT; Tan and Hong (2025) connect RL-tuned language models to EBMs theoretically. Across this work, energy is a deterministic scalar with no reliability signal; Gleave and Irving (2022) highlight this gap for reward models but use standard ensemble variance rather than structurally heterogeneous adapters. Our pairwise-preference learning connects to RLHF (Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022) and DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) but targets post-hoc verification of complete outputs; we further produce a distributional energy via a heterogeneous ensemble, decompose energy into learned and analytical components, and target structured multi-section outputs. A complementary line studies test-time compute allocation. Snell et al. (2025) show verifier-guided search can outperform scaling model parameters, Guo et al. (2025) show reinforcement learning alone can incentivise advanced reasoning, and Brown et al. (2024) identify candidate selection as the key bottleneck: pass@NN exceeds pass@1 but existing methods close the gap only partially. For structured planning, Lee et al. (2025) reach 95.6% on TravelPlanner via evolutionary search with Gemini 1.5 Flash, Xia et al. (2025) use reward modelling for agent generalisation, and Wang et al. (2025) combine multiple LLMs via mixture-of-agents. We address the selection bottleneck via energy-based reranking and the verification gap via analytical constraint penalties, using ensemble uncertainty to decide when selection is reliable.

3 Methodology

We propose a Distributional EBM (Fig. 2) with two stages: a quality scorer trained on contrastive candidate pairs (top), and inference-time candidate ranking with σ\sigma-triaged regeneration (bottom).

3.1 Problem Formulation

Let xx denote an input problem and let {y1,…,yN}\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{N}\} denote NN candidate structured outputs generated by frozen base LLMs via temperature sampling. We propose the decomposed energy function:

E⁡(x,y)=μquality​(x,y)+λ⋅Econstraint​(x,y),E(x,y)=\mu_{\text{quality}}(x,y)+\lambda\cdot E_{\text{constraint}}(x,y), (1)

and the selected candidate is the energy minimiser over the candidate pool 𝒴={y1,…,yN}\mathcal{Y}=\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{N}\}, y∗=arg​miny∈𝒴⁡E​(x,y)y^{*}=\argmin_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}E(x,y), where μquality​(x,y)\mu_{\text{quality}}(x,y) is the ensemble mean energy from the learned quality scorer, Econstraint​(x,y)E_{\text{constraint}}(x,y) is a sum of analytical penalty terms, and λ>0\lambda>0 controls their relative weight. The two components serve complementary roles: EqualityE_{\text{quality}} captures general reasoning quality learned from training data, while EconstraintE_{\text{constraint}} encodes task-specific rules that can be verified exactly without any learning.

3.2 Distributional Quality Scorer

We instantiate the quality scorer as an ensemble of KK EBMs sharing a frozen pretrained bidirectional Transformer encoder (Devlin et al., 2019; Warner et al., 2025). We choose an encoder over the now-standard causal-LM verifier so that a single [CLS] forward pass scores the whole [problem]||[candidate] pair jointly with bidirectional attention, at one to three orders of magnitude fewer parameters than CLM-based reward models or PRMs. To each member kk we attach a lightweight low-rank adapter (Houlsby et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2022) that modifies a subset of the encoder’s attention matrices, together with an independent energy head. Given a problem xx and candidate yy, the input is tokenised as inputk=[CLS]​x​[SEP]​y​[SEP]\text{input}_{k}=\texttt{[CLS]}\ x\ \texttt{[SEP]}\ y\ \texttt{[SEP]}. The frozen encoder, augmented by adapter kk, produces contextualised representations. The [CLS] representation 𝐡CLSk\mathbf{h}^{k}_{\text{CLS}} is passed through an MLP energy head producing a scalar Equalityk​(x,y)E^{k}_{\text{quality}}(x,y) (architecture in §C). Each adapter and energy head is trained independently; the frozen backbone is shared. The distributional output for candidate yy is the ensemble mean μquality​(x,y)=1K​∑k=1KEqualityk​(x,y)\mu_{\text{quality}}(x,y)=\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}E^{k}_{\text{quality}}(x,y) and standard deviation σquality​(x,y)=std​({Equality1,…,EqualityK})\sigma_{\text{quality}}(x,y)=\text{std}(\{E^{1}_{\text{quality}},\ldots,E^{K}_{\text{quality}}\}). The mean μquality\mu_{\text{quality}} is used for ranking (Eq. 1); the standard deviation σquality\sigma_{\text{quality}} drives the two-pass inference loop (Sec. 3.5) and provides a calibration signal for post-hoc analysis.

Diversity comes from three sources: structural heterogeneity (the KK adapters differ in rank, scaling factor, and target attention modules; Tab. 5 in §C), so disagreement reflects genuine epistemic uncertainty rather than seed variation (Fort et al., 2019; Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017); independent random initialisation per adapter; and 80% data bagging (Breiman, 1996). Trainable parameters per member (∼\sim3% of backbone) consist only of the LoRA weights and the energy head.

Theoretical justification. A natural question is what the distributional energy (μquality\mu_{\text{quality}}, σquality\sigma_{\text{quality}}) provides beyond a point-estimate scorer. We present two results that together justify the combination of decomposition and ensemble.

Proposition 3.1 (Ensemble ranking under correlated adapters).

Let each adapter kk correctly rank a random (correct, incorrect) pair with probability q>12q>\tfrac{1}{2}, and let ρ∈[0,1]\rho\in[0,1] denote the pairwise rank correlation between adapters. Under a Gaussian approximation for K≥5K\geq 5, the probability that the ensemble mean μquality\mu_{\text{quality}} correctly ranks the pair, and its K→∞K\to\infty limit (for any ρ>0\rho>0), are:

P​e​n​s​e​m​b​l​e​(K,q,ρ)=Φ⁡(K​(q−12)q⁡(1−q)​(1+(K−1)​ρ)),P∞​(q,ρ)=Φ⁡(q−12q⁡(1−q)​ρ)<1,P_{\emph{ensemble}}(K,q,\rho)=\Phi\!\left(\tfrac{\sqrt{K}\,(q-\tfrac{1}{2})}{\sqrt{q(1{-}q)(1+(K{-}1)\rho)}}\right),\quad P^{\infty}(q,\rho)=\Phi\!\left(\tfrac{q-\tfrac{1}{2}}{\sqrt{q(1{-}q)\,\rho}}\right)<1, (2)

where Φ\Phi is the standard normal CDF and P∞<1P^{\infty}<1 is a finite ceiling that no ensemble size can surpass unless ρ=0\rho=0.

Three consequences follow (proof and detailed analysis in §A). ∂P/∂ρ<0\partial P/\partial\rho<0, so structurally heterogeneous adapters (lower ρ\rho) strictly outperform same-architecture ensembles; when ρ=1\rho=1, Pensemble→qP_{\text{ensemble}}\to q regardless of KK; and for any ρ>0\rho>0 the ceiling in Eq. 2 is binding for moderate qq (e.g., narrative reasoning) and slack only when qq is near unity (e.g., K&K).

Proposition 3.1 justifies the ensemble for ranking. The following result justifies the decomposition for uncertainty: because EconstraintE_{\text{constraint}} is deterministic, σquality\sigma_{\text{quality}} reflects purely the epistemic uncertainty of the learned quality component, uncontaminated by constraint uncertainty.

Proposition 3.2 (Partitioned variance under energy decomposition).

Let E⁡(x,y)=μquality​(x,y)+λ⋅Econstraint​(x,y)E(x,y)=\mu_{\text{quality}}(x,y)+\lambda\cdot E_{\text{constraint}}(x,y) where EconstraintE_{\text{constraint}} is a deterministic analytical function. The predictive variance of the total energy decomposes as:

Var⁡(E)=Var⁡(Equality)+Var⁡(Econstraint)⏟= 0+2​Cov​(Equality,Econstraint)⏟= 0=σquality2.\mathrm{Var}(E)=\mathrm{Var}(E_{\text{quality}})+\underbrace{\mathrm{Var}(E_{\text{constraint}})}_{=\,0}+\underbrace{2\,\mathrm{Cov}(E_{\text{quality}},E_{\text{constraint}})}_{=\,0}=\sigma_{\text{quality}}^{2}. (3)

For a monolithic scorer EmonoE_{\text{mono}} that jointly learns both components, the predictive variance is Var⁡(Equalitymono)+Var⁡(Econstraintmono)+2​Cov​(Equalitymono,Econstraintmono)\mathrm{Var}(E_{\text{quality}}^{\text{mono}})+\mathrm{Var}(E_{\text{constraint}}^{\text{mono}})+2\,\mathrm{Cov}(E_{\text{quality}}^{\text{mono}},E_{\text{constraint}}^{\text{mono}}), which equals σquality2\sigma_{\text{quality}}^{2} only in the degenerate case that EconstraintmonoE_{\text{constraint}}^{\text{mono}} is learned exactly; otherwise the variance mixes constraint-prediction error into the uncertainty signal and is no longer interpretable as quality uncertainty.

This makes σquality\sigma_{\text{quality}} an interpretable uncertainty signal (quality only, with zero contribution from constraint verification), and motivates the σ\sigma-triage decision rule (Sec. 3.5): accept when σquality\sigma_{\text{quality}} and EconstraintE_{\text{constraint}} are both low, regenerate when either is high, abstain when σquality\sigma_{\text{quality}} is extreme. Proof and full implications are in §A.

3.3 Training

We train each member independently with the Bradley–Terry pairwise loss (Bradley and Terry, 1952) on bagged 80% subsets 𝒟k\mathcal{D}^{k} of training problems, where Yx+Y^{+}_{x} and Yx−Y^{-}_{x} are the correct/incorrect outputs for xx. The objective for member kk is:

ℒk=1|𝒟k|​∑x∈𝒟k1|Px|​∑(y+,y−)∈Pxlog⁡(1+exp⁡(Equalityk​(x,y+)−Equalityk​(x,y−))),\mathcal{L}^{k}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}^{k}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}^{k}}\frac{1}{|P_{x}|}\sum_{(y^{+},y^{-})\in P_{x}}\log\!\Big(1+\exp\!\big(E^{k}_{\text{quality}}(x,y^{+})-E^{k}_{\text{quality}}(x,y^{-})\big)\Big), (4)

where Px⊂Yx+×Yx−P_{x}\subset Y^{+}_{x}\times Y^{-}_{x} is a set of contrastive pairs sampled per problem, capped at a maximum count to prevent easy problems from dominating the gradient. Members are optimised separately (ℒ1,…,ℒK\mathcal{L}^{1},\ldots,\mathcal{L}^{K}); no parameters are shared across members beyond the frozen backbone. The loss pushes the energy of correct outputs below incorrect ones; the logistic form saturates naturally for well-separated pairs, avoiding the need for explicit energy regularisation.

Contrastive pairs are split at the problem level to prevent data leakage; labelling and hyperparameters are in Sec. 4.1. The trained ensemble is applied zero-shot to out-of-domain tasks; task-specific verification is handled entirely by EconstraintE_{\text{constraint}}.

3.4 Analytical Constraint Penalties

We define EconstraintE_{\text{constraint}} as a sum of analytical penalty terms, each encoding a specific task constraint: Econstraint​(x,y)=∑jwj⋅Cj​(x,y)E_{\text{constraint}}(x,y)=\sum_{j}w_{j}\cdot C_{j}(x,y), where CjC_{j} is the penalty for constraint jj and wjw_{j} is its weight. Each CjC_{j} returns 0 when the constraint is satisfied and a positive value proportional to the degree of violation. The constraint terms are deterministic: each is a direct computation over the parsed structured output with no learned parameters. They are also modular: adding or removing a constraint changes EconstraintE_{\text{constraint}} without affecting EqualityE_{\text{quality}} or requiring retraining. The specific constraint terms for each evaluation domain are defined in §E.

3.5 Two-Pass Inference with σ\sigma-Triage

We extend single-pass reranking with a two-pass inference loop driven by ensemble uncertainty and constraint satisfaction, recovering when no good candidate exists or the scorer is uncertain (Algorithm 1 in §F.5). Multiple frozen LLMs each generate NmN_{m} candidates via temperature sampling, which are pooled into the first-pass set 𝒴1\mathcal{Y}_{1} and scored. Each candidate receives μquality\mu_{\text{quality}} and σquality\sigma_{\text{quality}} from the K=5K{=}5 ensemble and EconstraintE_{\text{constraint}} from the analytical constraint checker. Let y1∗=arg​miny∈𝒴1⁡E​(x,y)y^{*}_{1}=\argmin_{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{1}}E(x,y) denote the first-pass selection. The system then takes one of three actions, governed by thresholds θσ<θabstain\theta_{\sigma}<\theta_{\text{abstain}}:

action​(y1∗)={acceptif ​σ≤θσ∧C=0,regenerateif ​σ≤θa∨C>0,abstainif ​σ>θa,\text{action}(y^{*}_{1})=\begin{cases}\mathrm{accept}&\text{if }\sigma\leq\theta_{\sigma}\;\land\;C=0,\\ \mathrm{regenerate}&\text{if }\sigma\leq\theta_{a}\;\lor\;C>0,\\ \mathrm{abstain}&\text{if }\sigma>\theta_{a},\end{cases} (5)

where σ=σquality​(y1∗)\sigma=\sigma_{\text{quality}}(y^{*}_{1}), C=Econstraint​(y1∗)C=E_{\text{constraint}}(y^{*}_{1}), and θa=θabstain\theta_{a}=\theta_{\text{abstain}}. On regenerate, constraint violations are formatted as natural-language feedback and used to draw N2N_{2} additional candidates 𝒴2\mathcal{Y}_{2}. The pooled set 𝒴=𝒴1∪𝒴2\mathcal{Y}=\mathcal{Y}_{1}\cup\mathcal{Y}_{2} is rescored, and the final selection is y∗=arg​miny∈𝒴⁡E​(x,y)y^{*}=\argmin_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}E(x,y), subject to a final abstention check on σquality​(y∗)\sigma_{\text{quality}}(y^{*}).

4 Experiments

Our experiments (Sec. 4.2) address five questions: (i) Is the bottleneck in structured LLM reasoning selection rather than generation? (ii) Does separating learned quality from analytical constraints improve correctness beyond either signal alone? (iii) Can ensemble disagreement reliably indicate when to trust, regenerate, or reject an output? (iv) Does the scorer learn genuine reasoning quality or exploit model-identity shortcuts? (v) Does the quality scorer transfer across reasoning domains without retraining? Extended results are in the Appendix (§F).

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets.

We evaluate across five benchmarks chosen for fundamentally different verification signals: math (GSM8K; Cobbe et al., 2021), narrative inference (MuSR; Sprague et al., 2024), multi-constraint planning (TravelPlanner; Xie et al., 2024b), executable code (TACO; Li et al., 2023), and formal logic (K&K; Xie et al., 2024a). We evaluate across all five domains together, where prior reranking work (Jiang and others, 2025; Lee et al., 2025) has typically focused on math or planning alone. GSM8K is partially contaminated (Yang et al., 2023; Oren et al., 2024), so we rely on MuSR (released 2024, post-dating all four generators’ pretraining) as the uncontaminated headline; MuSR results are reported on the full test split (151 problems across all three subsets), with per-subset breakdowns in §F.3. TravelPlanner contributes five analytical constraints (budget, connectivity, completeness, preferences, diversity) defining EconstraintE_{\text{constraint}}, verified against its sandbox database; K&K’s statement-consistency checker is a perfect verifier; TACO uses execution-based verification (we filter VERY_HARD with 0% solve rate). Primary metrics: pass@1 (single-sample correctness, the deployment-relevant figure) for GSM8K, MuSR, TACO, and K&K; mean violation score for TravelPlanner, since the strict zero-violation pass@1 compresses methods into a 0–30% band and hides the order-of-magnitude differences captured by the continuous score. Splits, EDA, per-model candidate quality, and examples are in §E (Tabs. 7 and 9); training data statistics in §D.

Candidate generators. We use four frozen generators chosen for open-weight access via OpenRouter and parameter-count diversity (7–26B): Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024), LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Gemma-4-26B-IT (Google DeepMind, 2026), and GPT-OSS-20B (OpenAI, 2025). Each produces 8 candidates per problem via temperature sampling (T=0.7T{=}0.7, top-p=0.95p{=}0.95 (Holtzman et al., 2020)), for N=32N{=}32 candidates per problem; all generation uses the OpenRouter API. Pass 2 adds N2=8N_{2}{=}8 candidates from Qwen-2.5-7B conditioned on constraint feedback.

Baselines. We compare against three groups: (1) heuristic selection from the candidate pool (Greedy at T=0T{=}0, random selection, Self-consistency majority vote, and an Oracle upper bound); (2) state-of-the-art frontier models (Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 (Anthropic, 2026), Qwen-72B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024)) which generate one deterministic answer at T=0T{=}0 rather than selecting from a pool; and (3) external learned selection methods that score the same candidate pool as our scorer: EORM (Jiang and others, 2025) (the closest prior energy-based method), Skywork-Reward-LLaMA-3.1-8B-v0.2 (Liu et al., 2024) (an 8B reward model), Math-Shepherd PRM (Wang et al., 2024) (a 7B step-level Process Reward Model), and LLM-as-Judge (Zheng et al., 2023) using Claude Sonnet 4.6 (frontier model scoring each candidate 1-10). Every learned baseline and frontier model in this comparison is substantially larger than our 149M-parameter scorer: Skywork at 8B (54×54\times), Math-Shepherd PRM at 7B (47×47\times), Qwen-72B (∼\sim483×\times), and the frontier Claude models are several hundred billion parameters, one to three orders of magnitude larger than ours.

Scorer backbone. The primary backbone is ModernBERT-base (Warner et al., 2025) (149M parameters, 8,192 token context); the long context accommodates MuSR narratives (3–6K characters) and full TravelPlanner itineraries without truncation. DeBERTa-v3-base (He et al., 2023) (86M parameters, 512 token context) is evaluated as an ablation; backbone comparison, adapter configurations, and DeBERTa-specific results are in §B and §F.1. The heterogeneous LoRA configuration follows Tab. 5 in §C with K=5K{=}5 adapters; LoRA and energy-head dropout are both 0.2.

Training. Each scorer is trained per-dataset via the Bradley–Terry loss in Eq. 4; candidates are labelled by task-specific verification (answer matching for GSM8K and MuSR, constraint-violation scoring for TravelPlanner, execution-based testing for TACO, and exact-match with statement-consistency checking for K&K). Optimiser: AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with cosine annealing (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017); learning rates 5×10−55\times 10^{-5} (K&K 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}); per-dataset batch sizes and stopping criteria in Tab. 6; all training on 3 NVIDIA L40S (46 GB).

Inference. For the energy decomposition (Eq. 1), we set λ=1.0\lambda{=}1.0 for GSM8K, MuSR, and TACO (where EconstraintE_{\text{constraint}} is not applied) and for K&K (where the exact statement-consistency checker requires no upweighting); λ=2.0\lambda{=}2.0 for TravelPlanner, where mean violation is the primary metric and heavier constraint weighting improves it. λ\lambda values were selected on a held-out validation split. The σ\sigma-triage rule (Eq. 5) uses thresholds θσ=0.8\theta_{\sigma}{=}0.8 and θabstain=1.5\theta_{\text{abstain}}{=}1.5, both chosen by grid search on a held-out validation split to maximise the pass@1 lift from regeneration while keeping the abstention rate below 10%. All evaluations use candidate shuffling (seed 42) to eliminate ordering bias.

4.2 Results

Our 149M Distributional EBM is the strongest non-oracle method on TravelPlanner, within 0.3 pp

of the best non-oracle on GSM8K, 4.3 pp on MuSR, near-greedy on TACO, and within 0.1 pp of perfect on K&K (Tab. 1), one to three orders of magnitude smaller than every other learned baseline. We organise the analysis around the five experimental questions: (i) selection vs. generation, (ii) decomposition, (iii) σ\sigma-triage, (iv) confounding, and (v) cross-domain transfer results are in Tab. 2.

Across the comparisons as shown in Tab. 1, Distributional EBM is the strongest non-oracle method on TravelPlanner, within 0.3 pp of the best non-oracle on GSM8K, within 4.3 pp on MuSR, near-greedy on TACO, and within 0.1 pp of perfect on K&K, while being one to three orders of magnitude smaller than every other learned baseline. Notes: ‡TP pass@1 (zero-violation) compresses methods to a 0–30% band: ours 28.0%, random 14.0%, self-consistency 12.0%. ∗Skywork and LLM-as-Judge TP violations are on a 20-problem subset matched to ground-truth scores (full pass@1: 21.1%, 55.0%). ♯EORM uses 256 candidates from 5 LLMs (8×8\times our budget). ♭LLM-as-Judge GSM8K is on a more lenient pool, see §E. --: baseline does not apply (math-only PRM/EORM).

(i) Selection vs. generation: before vs. after the verifier. On the same 32-candidate pool (Tab. 1): On MuSR, greedy 61.2% / oracle@32 86.1%; the Distributional EBM closes 26% of the gap to 67.7%, exceeding self-consistency (64.4%) and the 54×54\times larger 8B Skywork-Reward (Liu et al., 2024). LLM-as-Judge (Zheng et al., 2023) (Sonnet 4.6) reaches 73.5% (+5.8 pp) at 32 frontier-API calls per problem versus our single forward pass: roughly two orders of magnitude cheaper per accuracy point. On TACO, greedy reaches 86.4% (oracle 100.0%); the EBM lifts pass@1 to 88.6% (+2.2+2.2 pp over greedy, +42.0+42.0 pp over random, +52.2+52.2 pp over self-consistency whose majority vote on extracted code outputs is essentially uninformative), beating Skywork-Reward by +18.1+18.1 pp. On K&K, greedy already saturates from the strongest single generator (Gemma-4-26B at 100.0%); the multi-pool EBM achieves 99.9% (699/700) and dominates Skywork-Reward by +32+32 pp on 2-character puzzles to +47+47 pp on 8-character puzzles (Tab. 15). On GSM8K, contamination compresses the gap (greedy 91.8%, oracle 98.5%); the EBM reaches 97.0%, matching self-consistency within 0.3 pp and surpassing the 7B Math-Shepherd PRM (Wang et al., 2024) (94.2% with explicit step-level supervision) and EORM (Jiang and others, 2025) (90.7%; both restricted to math reasoning by construction). On TravelPlanner, where mean violation is the headline metric: greedy 0.098, EBM 0.046, a 53% reduction over greedy and 80% over random. The lift exists because the multi-generator pool has oracle headroom to convert: a Qwen-only pool collapses the ceiling on the uncontaminated reasoning tasks (+13.3+13.3/+52.2+52.2/+59.8+59.8 pp on MuSR/TACO/K&K; Tab. 12). Heterogeneous generators produce diverse error patterns and a higher oracle ceiling, giving the verifier more learning signal and more correct candidates to rank. Fig. 4 shows how the Distributional EBM front-loads correct candidates in its energy ranking; energy separation metrics are in §F.2.

(ii) Learned quality + analytical constraints. On TravelPlanner, the combined energy of Eq. 1 reaches 0.046 mean violation (Tab. 1), an 80% reduction over random (0.231); Skywork-Reward, lacking any structural verification, satisfies all constraints on only 21% of problems versus our method’s 28% pass@1. Ablating the two terms of Eq. 1 reveals complementary contributions: EqualityE_{\text{quality}} alone achieves 0.058 mean violation, EconstraintE_{\text{constraint}} alone achieves 0.038, and the combination (0.046) outperforms EqualityE_{\text{quality}} alone while adding learned quality dimensions that the constraint checker does not cover. Fig. 4 visualises the two-dimensional energy landscape; the two components agree on the top candidate in only 2% of problems, and in 28% of cases the combined energy selects a candidate that neither component would choose independently. On tasks without analytical constraints (GSM8K, MuSR, TACO), the method reduces to distributional μquality\mu_{\text{quality}} reranking alone and still provides substantial gains. TravelPlanner improvements over frontier models stem from the analytical constraint checker catching hallucinated transport routes (24-28% satisfaction for frontier models) that LLMs cannot self-detect. Independent LLM judges (Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6) corroborate the violation score and rate EBM-selected plans above oracle picks; full statistics in §F.6. Where structural verification is available, the verifier captures signal frontier models cannot self-detect; where pretraining-scale priors dominate (narrative, code semantics), frontier models lead: the two routes are complementary, not competing. Per-difficulty breakdowns for TACO and K&K are in §F.3.

(iii) Ensemble uncertainty as a decision signal. Two-pass σ\sigma-triage (Eq. 5) helps when pass-1 has headroom and feedback is structured: on TravelPlanner (Qwen-only generator pool, used to isolate the feedback effect from candidate diversity), it improves pass@1 from 74.0% to 80.0% (+6.0 pp). On TACO (deconfounded), two-pass is neutral (88.6%); on GSM8K, it is mildly counterproductive (−1.7-1.7 pp) precisely because the generator has memorised the answer and feedback distracts retrieval, a diagnostic feature: σ\sigma-triage detects which regime each task falls into rather than applying a one-size-fits-all loop. For selective prediction (Geirhos et al., 2020a), σquality\sigma_{\text{quality}} is task-dependent: on TravelPlanner, abstaining on 40% of problems raises pass@1 from 28.0% to 36.7% (+8.7 pp); on MuSR, σ\sigma does not signal correctness (AUROC 0.44), and the verifier is honest about where it cannot triage rather than offering an unreliable signal. The when-it-helps regime appears to depend on constraint-checkability and label discreteness rather than scoring task; we discuss the pattern in §F.5. Fig. 5 visualises the (μquality,σquality)(\mu_{\text{quality}},\sigma_{\text{quality}}) space; full results are in §F.5 and §F.4.

(iv) Reasoning quality vs. model-identity shortcuts. When candidate generators have different accuracy levels, the scorer may learn to identify which model produced each candidate rather than evaluating reasoning quality (Geirhos et al., 2020b). A cross-dataset confounding analysis (per-model pick distributions and cross-model correct-energy spreads) finds no fingerprinting on four of five tasks: GSM8K, MuSR, TravelPlanner, and K&K all show near-uniform picks and small spreads despite large generator accuracy gaps (full numbers in §F.8). On TACO the initial scorer fingerprinted strongly; a causal style-swap test confirms a formatting shortcut, mitigated via deep feature reweighting (DFR; Kirichenko et al., 2023) on the energy heads only (0.4% of parameters), restoring uniform picks at 88.6% pass@1 with +13.3+13.3 pp on HARD and +14.4+14.4 pp on UNKNOWN problems. The determining factor is output format, not generator accuracy gap: K&K has a more extreme accuracy split (88 pp) than TACO (74 pp), yet no fingerprinting, because reasoning text is stylistically similar across generators while code contains strong model-specific structural patterns.

(v) Cross-domain transfer. To test whether the quality scorer captures transferable reasoning signals, we evaluate each dataset’s checkpoint on every other dataset zero-shot (i.e., no retraining). Tab. 2 reports the key results. Three patterns emerge, all explained by training-data difficulty and signal-regime alignment. First, hard-to-easy transfer succeeds: a MuSR-trained scorer achieves 93.9% on GSM8K zero-shot (96.1% with the DeBERTa backbone variant; §F.7), within 3.4 pp of in-domain self-consistency (97.3%) without ever seeing a math problem. High candidate-accuracy entropy (MuSR 57%) forces the scorer to learn genuine reasoning-quality signals; high contamination (GSM8K 95% candidate accuracy) leaves few informative negatives, so the GSM8K-trained scorer reaches only 64.9% on MuSR – close to self-consistency (64.4%) but not exceeding it. Second, reasoning text and code are different signal regimes: reasoning-trained scorers (GSM8K, MuSR) do not transfer to TACO, but TACO→\rightarrowTravelPlanner transfers positively because code-execution labels capture quality signals that partially generalise to constrained planning (Tab. 2). Beyond cross-domain transfer, the verifier also transfers across generator distributions: a Qwen-only-trained scorer evaluated on a multi-model candidate pool reaches 69.5% pass@1 on MuSR (matching the multi-trained scorer’s 67.7%) and 90.5% on GSM8K, confirming the quality signal is not coupled to the training-pool generator style (§F.7). Calibration also transfers more broadly than ranking: a GSM8K-trained scorer achieves σ\sigma-AUROC of 0.79 on TravelPlanner zero-shot despite providing no ranking lift, suggesting ensemble disagreement captures a domain-general difficulty signal. The full transfer matrix including MATH-500 and a heatmap visualisation (Fig. 10) are in §F.7.

Limitations. (i) Generator ceiling: when no correct candidate exists, even perfect scoring cannot succeed (14% of MuSR; 58% of TravelPlanner at strict zero-violation). (ii) Format dependence: a GSM8K scorer achieves 65.6% on MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021), below random (68.4%), because it learned format signals rather than reasoning quality. (iii) Calibration limits: on MuSR, σ\sigma-AUROC is anti-correlated (0.44), making selective prediction counterproductive. (iv) Manual constraint design: EconstraintE_{\text{constraint}} must be authored per task; scaling directions in §G. (v) Single-round feedback: the two-pass loop adds only one regeneration round and is therefore less powerful than iterative refinement (Lee et al., 2025; Madaan et al., 2023). Full ablations are in §F.1.

5 Conclusion

Across the five reasoning tasks, three lessons emerge: (i) a 149M-parameter verifier orchestrating cheap 7–26B open generators outperforms single-shot Qwen-72B on every benchmark and matches frontier Claude models on constraint-heavy planning, demonstrating that the bottleneck in structured reasoning is selection, not parameter scale; (ii) the two routes are complementary: structural verification wins when constraints are checkable, while pretraining-scale priors win where they are not (web-scale corpora encode narrative and code-semantic priors a small scorer cannot match; analytical checking exposes hallucinations frontier models cannot self-detect); (iii) honest confounding analysis confirms the scorer learns content on four of five tasks, with the lone code-formatting shortcut on TACO fixable via last-layer retraining at no accuracy cost. The transferability of quality signals (a MuSR scorer reaching 93.9% on GSM8K zero-shot) suggests structured reasoning shares a common quality signature when training data is difficult enough to force genuine discrimination. Three directions follow: replacing the heterogeneous LoRA ensemble with epistemic deep learning for an axiomatically grounded energy in a single forward pass; extending single-round feedback to iterative energy-guided refinement; and richer structured feedback for tasks where two-pass currently fails on opaque signals (e.g., code execution errors).
